title: Latitude Band Finder: Which Zone Are You In?
description: Use the Latitude Band Finder to place any latitude in its band — tropical, temperate or polar — with the exact boundaries and widths. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, London at 51.5°N sits in the north temperate band, a zone about 4,793 km wide measured along the meridian between the tropics and the polar circles.
quick_answer: The Latitude Band Finder places any latitude into its classic band — tropical, temperate or polar — in either hemisphere. Enter a latitude or a place and read which band it falls in, the band's boundaries, and how wide that slice of the Earth really is.
steps_intro: Three bands per hemisphere, bounded by astronomy — here is where your latitude falls:

body.t: Why is Miami not tropical but Havana nearly is? Bands answer with geometry: the tropics end at 23.44°, and Miami at 25.8° misses them. The
Day length and Sun angle follow bands before they follow borders. A grower comparing sites at 35° and 55° is comparing different light regimes, and the band makes that visible.
Packing for a 'temperate' destination at 44°S — say Queenstown, New Zealand — means something precise about daylight and Sun height. Bands set honest expectations.
Articles love loose labels like 'polar Finland'. Finland's north crosses the Arctic Circle at 66.56° — the band finder verifies claims instead of repeating them.
The north temperate band runs from 23.44° to 66.56° — about 4,793 km of meridian arc. Most of the world's population lives in this one band and its southern twin.
Beyond the Arctic Circle there are only about 2,616 km of latitude left to the pole — yet that small cap holds the midnight Sun and polar night.

popular_table.title: The latitude bands and their true widths
popular_table.intro: Boundaries are set by Earth's axial tilt (about 23.44° today); widths are meridian arcs computed on WGS84.
popular_table.note: The tilt drifts slowly — about 0.47 arcseconds per year — so the tropics and polar circles creep toward the equator by roughly 15 metres a year. Band boundaries are astronomy, not administration.

faq: Earth's axial tilt. The tropics sit at ±(tilt) — today about 23.44° — and the polar circles at 90° minus the tilt, about 66.56°. Inside the tropics the Sun can be overhead; inside the polar circles it can stay up or down all day.
Are the bands the same as climate zones?
They are the astronomical skeleton under climate zones. Real climates add oceans, altitude and winds — a temperate-band desert and a temperate-band rainforest share a band, not a climate.
The tilt oscillates between about 22.1° and 24.5° over a 41,000-year cycle and is currently shrinking, so the tropics narrow by roughly 15 metres a year. Your lifetime moves them about a kilometre.
Which band has the most land?
The north temperate band, by a wide margin — it holds most of Europe, Asia and North America. The south temperate band is mostly ocean, which is why southern seasons feel maritime.
Can a place change bands without moving?

Effectively yes, over millennia, as the boundaries creep. With the tilt currently shrinking, the polar circles edge toward the poles (about 15 metres a year) and the tropics toward the equator — Arctic Circle roadside markers in Finland and Sweden have been re-sited for exactly this reason.
What band is the equator in?
The equator is the tropical band's centre line — the band extends 23.44° each side of it, a total width of about 5,186 km.
Directly. Only the polar bands get 24-hour days or nights; only the tropical band gets an overhead Sun; temperate bands get neither extreme — that is most of what 'temperate' means.
